items.text: Masking didn't fool other people. It fooled the system. The support you didn't get wasn't because you didn't need it — it's because the system was built to see traits you'd learned to hide.
items.rationale: Converts personal shame into structural critique in three sentences. No jargon, no hedging — the double-bind lands hardest when stated plainly.

items.text: There's a term for it now: 'visibility logic.' Support systems respond to visible autistic traits. If masking made you invisible to those systems, that's a structural flaw — not a personal one.
items.rationale: Names the 2026 academic concept in plain language, giving community members vocabulary for something they've felt but couldn't articulate. Distinct from draft 1 in that it leads with the term.

items.text: The problem was never that autistic people lack empathy. It's that neurotypical emotional expression was quietly made into the definition of empathy itself.
items.rationale: Moves the DEP conversation from individual defence to systemic critique in two sentences. Tight and quotable; the word 'quietly' does heavy lifting without overstating.

items.text: You're not failing at burnout recovery. You're rebuilding a self that was constructed around a role you didn't know you were playing. That takes longer than rest.
items.rationale: Directly addresses the 'just rest' advice and the shame of slow recovery. Plainspoken and short — the rhythm of three sentences mirrors the deliberateness the post is advocating for.

items.text: Late-diagnosed burnout recovery is slow not because something's wrong with you. It's because recovery isn't just rest — it's figuring out who you are when you're not masking. That's a different project entirely.
items.rationale: Companion to the reframe draft but opens on explicit exoneration. Different rhythm and entry point; reaches people who need the validation stated first before the reframe.

items.text: Late diagnosis grief isn't one wave. There's grief for younger you. For relationships. For the self-story you built to survive. And it resurfaces at milestones years later. That's not being stuck. The losses were real.
items.rationale: Names the layered, non-linear structure most content skips over. The list rhythm does the work of 'here are the layers' without becoming a listicle. Final line is exoneration, not pep talk.

items.text: If the strategies that help your child are the exact ones that wreck you, that's not a parenting failure. That's two nervous systems with incompatible needs in the same house — and it needs its own playbook.
items.rationale: Names the AuDHD parent/PDA child double-depletion bind without blame. Closes by legitimising the gap in existing resources rather than pretending a solution exists, which builds more trust.

items.text: Do you prefer 'Pathological Demand Avoidance' or 'Persistent Drive for Autonomy'? Not just semantics — what the name implies shapes how people respond to you.
items.rationale: Opens a live, consequential community debate without manufacturing conflict. Short and direct; the naming question is genuinely unsettled and the stakes are real.

items.text: PDA demand avoidance isn't defiance. For many PDAers, the demand itself registers as danger. That distinction changes everything about what actually helps.
items.rationale: 'For many PDAers' hedges correctly — no claim about all PDA experiences. Short and punchy; answers both the exhausted parent question and the PDA adult's internal one in the same frame.

items.text: Body doubling isn't a productivity hack. It's outsourcing the part of executive function that neurotypical brains handle internally. A 2024 study found 85% of neurodivergent participants completed more tasks with it. Free options exist.
items.rationale: Grounds a community-discovered practice in a reframe and a concrete data point, then closes with the most actionable word possible. Earns its length by being genuinely useful.
items.sensitivity_flag: The 85%/2024 study figure is reported only via secondary sources in the briefing; the primary study is not directly linked. Verify the citation and sample context before publishing — the figure is plausible but the methodology is unconfirmed here.

items.text: You don't have to disclose a diagnosis to ask for a workplace accommodation. Describe the barrier: 'I lose track of verbal-only instructions.' In many jurisdictions, that's enough to require a response.
items.rationale: Directly addresses fear-of-disclosure as a barrier. 'In many jurisdictions' is honest about limits without undercutting the central empowering claim. Specific example grounds it immediately.
items.sensitivity_flag: Legal accuracy varies significantly by country and employer size. 'In many jurisdictions, enough to require a response' is hedged but should be reviewed by someone with employment law knowledge before publishing — particularly for UK/US/AU audiences where the rules differ.

items.text: If you were diagnosed autistic as an adult, which hit harder — the diagnosis itself, or slowly realising what it explains about the years before? I think the answer says a lot about which layer of grief you're in.
items.rationale: Opens the late-diagnosis grief conversation as a genuine invitation rather than a statement. Seeds the 'layered grief' concept without requiring a full explanation, inviting comment-thread depth.
